mcqs.question: Why should you re-derive complexity from the code on screen every time, even when you're confident you already know the answer?
options: A memorized complexity for "this kind of problem" can silently mismatch the actual code if you added or changed something mid-solution
Complexity notation changes depending on the programming language used
Re-deriving isn't actually necessary if the initial plan didn't change
Interviewers always penalize fast answers regardless of correctness
mcqs.explanation: Mid-solution edits — an extra loop for an edge case, an added sort — can change the real complexity without you noticing, so re-deriving from the actual code catches that. Complexity notation is language-independent, and confidence in the original plan doesn't protect against changes made while coding.

mcqs.question: Why is calling BFS/DFS "O(n²)" on a graph potentially misleading?
options: The correct complexity is always O(V) alone, ignoring edges entirely
Graph traversal complexity depends only on the traversal algorithm's implementation language
BFS/DFS is never O(n²) under any circumstances
It collapses two independent variables — vertices and edges — into one, hiding that a sparse graph runs nearly linear while a dense one doesn't
mcqs.explanation: The honest bound is O(V + E); writing n² implicitly assumes vertices and edges scale the same way, which erases the real difference between a sparse and a dense graph. Ignoring edges entirely would be equally wrong, since edge count directly drives the work in most traversals.

mcqs.question: What's the most complete way to describe the cost of appending to a dynamic array?
options: It depends entirely on which programming language implements the array
O(1) always — resizing is rare enough to ignore
Amortized O(1): most appends are O(1), the occasional O(n) resize is averaged out because resizes happen exponentially less often as the array grows
O(n) worst case, full stop — the occasional resize dominates
mcqs.explanation: Amortized analysis exists exactly to give a fair single number for this lumpy cost — most calls are cheap, and the rare expensive resize is smoothed out over the sequence of appends. Quoting only O(n) overstates the typical case and quoting only O(1) glosses over the resize entirely.

mcqs.question: Why is stating "this is O(n log n), which matches the proven lower bound for comparison-based sorting" a stronger answer than just stating O(n log n) alone?
options: It shows you know your solution can't be meaningfully improved without changing the model, which is the senior-level version of the answer
It's stronger only because it uses more technical vocabulary
Because Ω notation is always required alongside O notation by convention
It isn't stronger — the lower bound is irrelevant to interview scoring
mcqs.explanation: Knowing where your answer sits relative to a proven lower bound demonstrates you understand the theoretical ceiling, not just that you found *an* answer — that context is exactly what distinguishes a senior-level response. It isn't about vocabulary for its own sake, and there's no blanket convention requiring both notations together.

mcqs.question: A candidate adds a `.sort()` call mid-solution to fix a bug, then states the complexity they had planned before that change. Why does this read worse than simply not knowing the complexity?
options: Adding a sort call is always disallowed in coding interviews
It only matters if the interviewer explicitly asks about the sort call
It doesn't read worse — interviewers only check the final numeric answer
It suggests the stated complexity was never actually derived from the code, but recited from an earlier plan — a reasoning gap, not just a knowledge gap
mcqs.explanation: A stale complexity claim reveals the number was recited rather than derived from the actual code — a deeper problem than admitting uncertainty, since it undermines trust in every other claim made during the round. Sort calls are a normal part of many solutions, and this issue matters regardless of whether the interviewer happens to ask about it directly.
